query: Simliar books like "I, Robot" from Isaac Asimov.
answer:
Based on Hacker News comments, there are several books that share themes with Asimov’s *I, Robot*—especially around robots, artificial intelligence, and the ethical/moral problems that arise.

A few direct recommendations from the community:

- **Rudy Rucker’s *Live Robots*** — As user cliffwarden puts it, “Please do yourself a favor and read some of Ruckers sci-fi books! Live Robots is a great entry” [[3]](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=42164040).
- **Walter Tevis’s *Mockingbird*** — User nicwolff recommends it, describing it as “one of my favorite books” and noting how it captures “how eager mankind is to hand over all intellectual labor to the robots.” They also mention a plot point where a last surviving level 9 robot hires the first man who has learned to read in 400 years to translate silent film title cards [[4]](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=45585585).
- **Charles Stross’s *Saturn’s Children*** — User KineticLensman says they enjoyed “charles Stross’s take on the laws of robotics in Saturns Children, an SF which explores the problems that robots face with the laws after humankind has gone extinct” [[8]](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=37805123).
- **Adam Wiśniewski-Snerg’s *Robot*** — User kataklasm recommends it “in a similar vein,” explaining that it’s about “the relationship between humans and artificial life/intelligence,” with the central theme of wondering whether you’re “real” in an artificial world. They caution that it’s “not the easiest read and can be quite dark at times” [[9]](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=44177717).

Several users also point out that Asimov’s own wider **Robot series** is the natural continuation if you liked *I, Robot*. As one comment notes, “Asimov's robot series explains everything from the basics to the nuances rather well” [[2]](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=35052400). Another adds that “almost the entirety of Asimov's Robots canon is a meditation on how the Three Laws of Robotics as stated are grossly inadequate” [[11]](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=46125705), so if you enjoyed the moral puzzles in *I, Robot*, the rest of Asimov’s robot stories continue that thread.

query: Books, substacks, and blogs about the specific patterns and practices of effective project management as a software engineer in big tech
answer:
The Hacker News community shared a rich set of books, blogs, substacks, and other resources for software engineers wanting to improve project management and technical leadership, especially in big-tech settings. Here’s a consolidated guide based on those comments.

## Books on Project Management and Technical Leadership

Several users specifically recommended books that are widely considered practical and effective:

- **The Manager’s Path by Camille Fournier** – Mentioned by multiple users. As user romanhn puts it, “The Manager's Path by Camille Fournier is a great practical book on engineering management” [[8]](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=35032917). User bwh2 also recommends it, specifically suggesting readers “read the chapter on being a Tech Lead” [[2]](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=35154550).

- **Making Work Visible** – Recommended by bwh2 as one of their favorite books for managing software projects and technical leadership [[2]](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=35154550).

- **Accelerate** – Also from bwh2’s favorites list, likely useful for understanding the metrics and practices that drive high-performing software teams [[2]](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=35154550).

- **Peopleware: Productive Projects and Teams** – User leetrout calls it “my favorite book when it comes to practical advice on managing software development teams” [[11]](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=37482909).

- **Software Engineering at Google** – User mplutecki describes it as “The best book about software engineering I found so far,” linking to the freely available resource from Google’s Abseil project [[12]](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=41417962).

## Blog Posts and Articles

Several comments point to a widely referenced deep-dive on how big tech actually runs projects:

- User rcarr shares the article “How Big Tech Runs Tech Projects and the Curious Absence of Scrum” with the note, “This is always a good read” [[1]](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=34875903). User cpeterso expands on the same article: “There is no best approach, but this article highlights some common aspects from a survey of 100+ tech companies’ approaches to project management” [[10]](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=37289771). The article is from the Pragmatic Engineer blog and is a key reference for big-tech-specific PM patterns.

## Reading Lists and Resource Aggregators

- User bwh2 points to their own book-review site focused on tech leads: “My website has more book reviews on this topic: https://www.briansnotes.io/audience/tech-lead/” [[2]](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=35154550).

- User pixelmonkey highlights a blog post reviewing software engineering books, organized into six sections. The three relevant sections are:
  - “Debugging dysfunctional product cultures”
  - “The psychology of deep work”
  - “Programmer mindset and philosophy”
  Link: https://amontalenti.com/2020/11/28/definitive-reading-list [[5]](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=39061039)

- User aemre shares a large GitHub repository of engineering management resources: “There is a big list of resources related to engineering management which might be relevant: https://github.com/ryanburgess/engineer-manager” [[6]](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=39338678).

## Substack Newsletters and Blogs

For ongoing reading, users also recommended substacks and engineering blogs:

- User rafapaez mentions that there are “a lot of great newsletters nowadays about People Management and Engineering Leadership” and shares their own Substack on that topic: https://rafapaez.substack.com/ [[9]](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=39340289).

- User brianmz highlights several high-quality company engineering blogs: “Multiple high quality company engineering blogs including https://netflixtechblog.com/, https://www.uber.com/en-US/blog/engineering/, DoorDash etc.” They also mention https://techtalksweekly.io/ for conference talks and podcasts, https://ciechanow.ski/ for interactive technical articles, and https://jvns.ca/ for great technical content [[7]](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=46784514).

## A Note of Caution from the Community

Not all comments focus on recommended resources. User kingkongjaffa offers a more skeptical take on formal project-management frameworks in tech:

> “Honestly I kind of rail against the suitability of traditional Project management thinking in tech. Beyond knowing: who does what, and by when, and for how much $$ the project management frameworks are largely fluff.”

They argue that a decent task list, deadlines, a Gantt chart, and a stakeholder RACI matrix may be all you truly need, and that the rest is mainly soft skills and stakeholder alignment [[4]](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=38139367). This is a useful counterpoint for engineers who want to avoid getting lost in heavyweight PM processes.

---

Overall, the community recommends a blend of:
- Foundational books like *The Manager’s Path*, *Making Work Visible*, *Accelerate*, and *Peopleware*.
- The Pragmatic Engineer article on how big tech actually manages projects.
- Curated reading lists and engineering-management resource aggregators.
- Engineering leadership substacks and company engineering blogs for ongoing learning.

Given the breadth of links, you can start with the Pragmatic Engineer article for the big-tech view, *The Manager’s Path* for practical engineering-management advice, and the GitHub curated list if you want a larger catalog of resources.

The Hacker News discussion highlights several notable trends in AI research, ranging from rapid advances in large language models and agents to shifts in industry leadership, investment, and societal impact.

## Rapid Progress and Exponential Growth
Multiple users point to the speed of AI development. As **Laaas** puts it, "almost every day now we see a new breakthrough in AI. Exponential technological growth is hard to keep track of" [[2]](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=35154597). Similarly, **pifm_guy** notes that "there have been some pretty big advances in the last few months in machine learning" [[5]](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=34309502), while **martinmusio7** calls the future "dynamic and exciting," based on a review of research papers and industry strategies [[8]](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=40130428).

## Core Research Areas
The conversation identifies several major research directions.

- **Foundational models and LLMs**: A ChatGPT-generated overview shared by **neduma** includes foundational models like GPT-4 and BERT, computer vision, reinforcement learning, AI ethics, quantum machine learning, healthcare, robotics, climate change, explainability, and emerging areas [[1]](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=38661637).
- **AI agents**: **cobusgreyling** explains that "AI Agents are agentic software applications which primarily live within a digital environment," relying on LLM skills like decomposing problems and reasoning; the Self-Discover approach lets LLMs compose their own reasoning structures [[6]](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=41487389). **acmerfight** expands on this, describing LLM agents as "the upcoming breakthrough in AI," covering topics such as reasoning, planning, tool use, retrieval-augmented generation, code generation, robotics, safety, and multi-agent collaboration [[10]](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=41912068).
- **Transformers and diffusion models**: **seydor** wryly observes that while AI research is increasing exponentially, "most of the list is transformers & stablediffusion," and argues that open-source tools like oobabooga and automatic1111 "are doing more to spread AI than many of those papers" [[7]](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=36074616).
- **Outside deep learning**: **nl** highlights "zero-knowledge techniques" as the most interesting AI work outside deep learning, though still nascent [[11]](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=35036578).

## Structural Trends and Impacts
**evo_9** summarizes the AI Index Report 2023, which reveals major structural trends:

- Industry now leads academia in releasing significant machine learning models.
- Traditional benchmarks are showing performance saturation.
- AI is accelerating scientific progress, but incidents related to AI misuse are rising.
- Private investment in AI decreased in 2022 for the first time in a decade.
- AI adoption by companies has plateaued, though adopting firms see cost and revenue benefits.
- Policymaker interest is growing, with more AI-related bills passed.
- Public attitudes vary: Chinese citizens are most positive about AI, while Americans are more skeptical [[3]](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=35440109).

## Underlying Enablers
**bmitc** offers a grounded perspective: "Machine learning has been around for decades. The real breakthrough has been the massive increase in compute power, the ubiquity of distributed systems, and the amount of data available" [[12]](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=35324439). This suggests that infrastructure advances, rather than purely algorithmic novelty, are driving much of the current momentum.

## Cautionary Notes
Some commenters inject skepticism. **jruohonen** wonders whether 1980s/1990s pop science about predictability, such as Poincaré’s ideas on initial conditions, "might have something relevant to say with respect to the current day's AI craze" [[4]](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=39064936). And **paulddraper** recalls that "machine learning became quite the buzzword in 2016(?)" [[9]](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=36944614), implying cycles of hype.

Overall, the HN comments paint a picture of a fast-moving field dominated by LLMs and agents, with growing attention to real-world impacts, infrastructure, and the gap between research output and broader societal adoption.

query: how to keep up with AI research
answer:
The Hacker News community offers a range of strategies, from curated newsletters to “learn by building,” plus a healthy warning not to chase every hype cycle.

**1. You don’t necessarily need to “keep up” with everything**  
Some commenters argue that trying to track the entire AI frontier is counterproductive. As user rglover puts it, “You don't need to 'keep up,' you just need to loosely pay attention to identify things/features that will make you more productive, test them out, and keep what actually works.” They add that listening to researchers who dismiss wild AI claims is more useful than blind hype, and “If it's actually revolutionary, you'll hear about it on HN” [[1]](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=44609960).

**2. Use curated newsletters, sites, and daily digests**  
Several users recommend specific sources to stay informed efficiently. User ncvdv suggests checking sites like `news.bensbites.co`, using niche search filters, and browsing HN’s top pages, plus following organizations such as OpenAI, StabilityAI, and DeepMind on Twitter along with AI researchers in those communities [[4]](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=35849806). User Johnnyang66 recommends spending “five minutes a day on https://infobuzz.ai,” saying it manually curates AI news from major outlets from the past 24 hours [[7]](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=44611424). User mesonyktio lists resources like The Batch newsletter, YouTube channels such as AI Breakdown and AI Explained, podcasts like Last Week in AI and Super Data Science, and people like Karpathy and Andrew Ng to follow [[8]](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=40073371).

**3. Follow the right people and communities on social platforms**  
User quantadev recommends getting on Twitter to follow leading AI individuals, and watching YouTube channels dedicated to AI research [[3]](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=41558888). User gregtim suggests joining online communities and forums such as GitHub, Reddit, and Stack Overflow, attending conferences and workshops, and subscribing to publications like AI News, MIT Technology Review, and TechCrunch [[6]](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=35052385). Mesonyktio also mentions Discord servers like Hugging Face and LLMOps.space, plus Reddit communities like r/artificial and r/datascience [[8]](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=40073371).

**4. Build things and learn by doing**  
User cs702 offers a deeper approach: “Build something of personal interest to you. Start by looking for similar open-source projects online. Look at the online posts of the authors. Then look for the papers that you think will be useful for your project.” They caution against relying on programmatic “most important papers” lists, citing the amount of hype, propaganda, and citation hacking around new AI research [[10]](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=38654333).

**5. Continuous learning and experimentation**  
User gregtim emphasizes that staying on top of AI within software development requires continuous learning, industry events, online communities, training programs, and experimenting with tools and techniques. Collaboration with experts and sharing best practices are also key [[9]](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=34981532).

In short, the community’s advice ranges from “don’t bother trying to keep up with everything” to “use a small set of curated daily sources, follow key researchers, and most importantly, build something real with AI to ground your understanding.”
